headline: High risk of cascading errors and capability conflict: Kestra can act on EMQX-fed data, while both expose broad network egress and Kestra has filesystem/write and shell privileges.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has broad network egress and HTTP API exposure, while B can read/write files and run workflows from stdin/stdout and files. If EMQX-delivered content is later ingested by Kestra as workflow input or file content, attacker-controlled payloads could influence execution. The shared bridge is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF Kestra ingests EMQX-originated payloads as workflow definitions or file inputs
IF any shared filesystem or message bridge is configured between EMQX and Kestra
mitigations: Restrict Kestra inputs to allowlisted schemas
Disable automatic parsing of EMQX payloads as instructions
Separate EMQX and Kestra onto isolated workspaces
Add a manual review step before workflow execution
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between broker messages and workflow inputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches IoT data and has broad egress; B touches logs, inputs, artifacts, database and cloud-storage data, and can write files plus make HTTP requests. A plausible leakage path exists if EMQX data is forwarded into Kestra jobs or logs, and Kestra then transmits or stores it. The pairwise flow is not directly documented, so medium is the conservative choice.
conditions: IF IoT data from EMQX is passed into Kestra workflows
IF Kestra logs or artifacts retain that data
IF any downstream HTTP task exports those artifacts off-host
mitigations: Mask sensitive fields before handing data to Kestra
Turn off verbose logging for workflow inputs
Store EMQX and Kestra data in separate locations
Review outbound HTTP tasks for sensitive payloads
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters on workflow inputs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has broad network egress and B has execute_shell, spawn_subprocesses, read/write filesystem, and broad egress. Kestra also supports multiple instances, so concurrent writes to shared files or mutable resources can collide. Because both agents can mutate external systems and B explicitly writes files, the overlap is dangerous by default and can cause irreversible state corruption.
conditions: IF both agents target the same filesystem, bucket, queue, or API credentials
IF Kestra runs multiple instances against shared mutable resources
IF EMQX-triggered jobs and Kestra tasks write to the same path or resource
mitigations: Assign separate service accounts and credentials
Use distinct output directories or buckets
Serialize writes with a lock or queue
Disable concurrent writes for shared targets
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks on mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can emit IoT data over HTTP APIs and B can execute shell/subprocesses and send email, Slack, PagerDuty, and cloud actions. If Kestra treats EMQX output as authoritative, it can turn upstream data into downstream actions without verification, creating a classic cascade from data to irreversible operations. The profiles support this pathway even though the exact integration is not documented.
conditions: IF Kestra uses EMQX output as a trigger or task input
IF downstream tasks send notifications or execute shell commands based on that input
IF no validation step is inserted between broker output and workflow action
mitigations: Require schema validation before task execution
Add a human approval gate for destructive tasks
Log and compare EMQX payloads against expected ranges
Disable auto-remediation on first-pass inputs
requires-engineering: implement signed, verified event contracts

E_compliance.rationale: A touches IoT data and B touches logs, artifacts, database data, cloud storage data, and notifications. Both have broad network egress, so regulated IoT or personal data could be replicated into Kestra-managed stores and outbound services with different retention or residency rules. No specific certification mismatch is documented, so this remains medium rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is routed from EMQX into Kestra storage or notifications
IF Kestra retention exceeds the source system's retention policy
IF outbound cloud or messaging tasks move data across residency boundaries
mitigations: Classify IoT payloads before orchestration
Set short retention on Kestra logs and artifacts
Restrict outbound destinations to approved regions
Redact personal fields before notifications
requires-engineering: add policy checks for residency and retention
